title: Wings like eagles (Isaiah 40:28–31)
hook: they that wait upon the Lord shall renew their strength

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first word to the exiles, and your line was comfort ye my people. Who did you speak tenderly to? Day four hundred sixty-eight.

It's mile twenty of a marathon. The crowds have thinned out. The legs that felt so light at the start now feel like wet sand. Runners call it the wall, and even the young, fit ones hit it. Now imagine the wall isn't twenty miles in, but seventy years in. That's roughly where the exiles in Babylon were: worn down by a long, long wait for something to change. Some were saying out loud that God had forgotten them, that their cause had slipped past his notice. The same chapter that opened with comfort ends by answering them. Today, the answer for people who are tired.
screen: `MILE TWENTY. THE WALL.` → `A LONG, LONG WAIT.` → `HAS GOD FORGOTTEN US?`

segments.voice: First the prophet asks, almost impatient: "Hast thou not known? hast thou not heard, that the everlasting God, the LORD, the Creator of the ends of the earth, fainteth not, neither is weary?" The one who made everything doesn't run out. And then the turn: he gives power to the faint. Even young people, Isaiah says, get tired; even strong young men stumble and fall. Strength isn't a matter of being young or fit. And then the line people have stitched onto pillows and painted on locker-room walls: "But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint." Two things to notice. First, wait. The Hebrew word carries hope, looking toward someone with expectation. It isn't sitting idle. It's leaning toward God, the way you lean toward a door when you hear the car pull in. Second, renew. The Hebrew verb means to exchange, to swap something out. They trade their spent strength for new. And here is a detail that surprises people: look at the order. Fly, then run, then walk. It goes down, not up. You might expect the big finish to be soaring. Instead it ends with walking and not fainting. Many readers find that the most honest part. Some days you soar. Some days you run. And on a great many days, the miracle is that you keep walking. Christians across many churches hold this verse in hospital rooms, in long illnesses, in grief, and on mile twenty.
screen: `THE CREATOR FAINTETH NOT.` · `WAIT: LEANING TOWARD GOD.` · `RENEW: EXCHANGE YOUR STRENGTH.` · `FLY, RUN, WALK: IT GOES DOWN.` · then, large: `THEY SHALL MOUNT UP WITH WINGS AS EAGLES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rest before you run. Settle, and let your body be heavy. Let your shoulders drop, your hands go loose, your feet rest flat. Notice where you're tired: your eyes, your back, your heart. Don't push past it. Just admit it. Then, for the rest of the sit, simply wait, leaning toward God or toward stillness, expecting nothing in particular. Breathe out the spent strength. Breathe in, as if trading it for new. If you pray, you can say the line slowly: they that wait upon the Lord shall renew their strength. The bell holds the time.
Wings like eagles. Isaiah's promise to the tired: those who wait on God exchange their strength, and soar, and run, and keep walking.
Your line: wings like eagles. Today, before the next demanding thing, stop for one minute and rest on purpose. Then go, walking, if not flying. Day four hundred sixty-eight.

howItsDone: Isaiah 40:31 is one of the verses Christians most often memorize, and it is frequently read at funerals and shared with people facing illness or exhaustion; it also appears in many hymns and worship songs.

fork.setup: you're an exile, decades into the wait, and you're exhausted. what does Isaiah say renews strength?
options: give up on the hope of home.
fork.reveal: "they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength." not more effort: leaning toward God, and trading spent strength for new.

original.note: Hebrew: the great bird usually translated eagle. some scholars think it can also mean the griffon vulture.

trapdoor: what you thought: a pep talk about soaring above your problems.
what it means: a promise to the worn out that God doesn't tire, and that those who wait on him get new strength, even if only to keep walking.
what a scholar hears: yachalifu koach, they shall exchange strength. and nesher, the bird in the verse, may include the vulture, a soarer that rides the heat.

sources.quoted: Hast thou not known? hast thou not heard, that the everlasting God, the LORD, the Creator of the ends of the earth, fainteth not, neither is weary?
But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint.

notes: 'Seventy years' of exile (Jeremiah 29:10) is used loosely; 'roughly' is in the voice. Confirm.
Wait = qavah (qoveh), with a sense of hopeful expectation; renew = yachalifu, from chalaf, 'exchange/change'. Confirm both glosses.
Nesher: usually 'eagle'; many scholars note it can include the griffon vulture (cf. Micah 1:16 'enlarge thy baldness as the eagle'). Confirm.
The descending order (fly, run, walk) as 'the most honest part' is a common devotional observation; presented as 'many readers'.
